description: The dip is the upper body's squat, and its score is decided at the most tendon-dependent joint you own. Your shoulder is held together by cables, not by bone, and this test grades every one of them. Today you get your dip number, the anatomy under it, and the thirty-day plan to raise it safely.

scenes.narration: Set up between bars. | Or two sturdy chairs. | Grip and lift yourself. | Arms fully straight. | Lower down slowly. | Upper arm reaches parallel. | Press back up. | Count clean reps only. | No bouncing below. | No half presses. | Stop when form breaks. | That number is yours. | Write it down. | This test is an audit | of your shoulders. | The joint held together | by tendons alone. | At the end today | I show you why | the cables decide here. | Keep your number. | Elbows track back. | Chest stays proud. | Every rep identical.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN PRESSING AND OWNING
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Fifteen full-depth dips is where pressing becomes owning. Under five is where most adults honestly live, because almost nobody trains this movement with real depth. Five to fifteen means the pressing chain works and the shoulder system is learning its job. Over twenty-five full reps is gymnast territory, where bodyweight has become a warm-up weight. Keep your number next to that line, whatever it is. The dip is called the upper body squat for a reason, and the reason your number stops where it does lives in the strangest joint you own.
scenes.sub: under 5 reps: the normal start - over 25: gymnast territory

beats.text: A BALL ON A GOLF TEE

scenes.narration: Understand your shoulder and the dip makes sense. Most joints are sockets that hold their bones by shape. Your shoulder is not. It is a large ball resting on a shallow tee, an arrangement built for freedom, not security. What actually holds it together is a team of tendons, the rotator cuff and its partners, constantly adjusting tension to keep the ball centered while bigger muscles produce force around it. Now place that joint in a dip. At the bottom, your upper arm sits behind your body, the front of the shoulder stretches under load, and the chest and triceps tendons take heavy tension while the cuff works overtime to keep everything centered. It is the most tendon-dependent moment in upper-body training. This is why dip numbers stall for reasons that feel mysterious. The chest is willing. The triceps are willing. The limiting factor is a stability system made of cables, quietly deciding how much force it will allow before it pulls the emergency brake. Train the cables and the brake releases. Ignore them and the number stays frozen no matter how hard you press. The triceps tendon deserves its own sentence. It is the single cable that straightens your elbow, and in the dip it works at the longest muscle lengths and the deepest joint angles in pressing. The lockout that feels like a formality is the tendon finishing the job under full tension. Weak there, and reps die one inch from the top, fully pressed and nowhere to go.

The bottom of the dip deserves respect, because it is both the training and the test. Down there, the chest tendon and the front shoulder structures sit at long length under your full bodyweight. Tendons adapt to exactly this combination of length and load, which is why full-depth, controlled dips remodel the pressing system in a way shallow reps never touch. Shallow reps are not a safer version of the exercise. They are a different, smaller exercise that skips the position where adaptation lives. Control is the whole game. A two-second descent gives the cuff time to organize and the tendons time to align with the force. A dropped, bouncing descent throws the load onto structures that were not ready to receive it, and the shoulder keeps the receipts. The same logic explains why gymnasts, the dip's masters, look serene at depths that make lifters nervous. Their tendon systems were built by years of slow, exact repetitions. Serenity at the bottom is not talent. It is tissue that has been properly introduced to the position, thousands of times. Age makes the point from the other direction. Shoulder tendons lose stiffness and blood supply across the decades, which is why pressing positions feel riskier at fifty than at twenty. The hopeful reading of that fact is that the tissue remains trainable at every age studied. It simply asks for slower introductions and more patience between doses.

Your advantage should be familiar by now, but pressing has its own version of it. A dip lifts your body and nothing else, so every kilo you do not carry is a discount on every rep. The shoulder's tendon team is roughly the same size in you as in a much heavier man, yet it is asked to stabilize and press far less mass. The result is more clean reps per session, and clean reps at full depth are the precise stimulus the system remodels from. The heavy trainee's dip session ends early, his shoulders taxed by absolute load. Yours keeps going, stacking the slow, controlled repetitions that build cuff teamwork and tendon stiffness together. There is a reason the athletes synonymous with this movement are gymnasts, compact and lean, pressing their bodies like the weight is a rumor. Pressing your own body is a relative-strength sport wearing a strength costume. In a relative-strength sport, the light athlete is not the underdog. He is the specialist the event was designed for, whether the event admits it or not.
Press with me. Four rounds of thirty seconds of dips, forty-five seconds of rest. Full depth, two seconds down, shoulders away from your ears. Stop any rep that pinches. Go.

Your plan, and the three mistakes that freeze dip numbers. Mistake one is shallow depth, pressing from a quarter bend and counting it. The tendon never visits the position it needs to adapt to. Mistake two is shrugging, shoulders climbing to your ears as you tire, which hands the work to your neck and abandons the cuff. Mistake three is bouncing, dropping into the bottom and rebounding out, which turns a controlled load into a collision. One safety rule above all: if you feel a sharp pinch in the front of your shoulder, stop, reduce the depth, and build up gradually. Earn depth like this. Start with support holds, simply holding the top position strongly. Add slow negatives, lowering over five seconds with feet assisting the way up. Then partial reps, then full ones. A little practice most days beats a weekly war, and in a month the bottom position will feel like a place you live, not a place you visit. Keep a simple rule for depth: only go as deep as you can return from with perfect control and zero pinch. That depth will deepen on its own as the tissue adapts, which is the only safe way depth has ever been earned.

scenes.label: RETEST - SAME BARS, FULL DEPTH
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under five: the normal start, with the fastest progress in the whole pressing world ahead of you. Five to fifteen: the chain is learning and the shoulder system is organizing itself rep by rep. Fifteen to twenty-five: you own the press, full depth and full control. Over twenty-five: gymnast territory, where your bodyweight has become light equipment. Write your number in the comments. Just the number. In thirty days we return to the same bars at the same depth, and your shoulders will report what their cables rebuilt.
scenes.sub: comment your number below - then beat it

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, the same bars and a number that tells the truth about your shoulders. Subscribe for the retest and for the next test in this series. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
